title: Which AWS ETL tool fits you?

questions.hint: The source cuts the list in half right away.

options.label: SaaS apps such as Salesforce
options.why: your source is a SaaS app: DMS reads databases, Firehose takes event streams, and OLake Go moves databases

options.label: A live database
options.why: your source is a database: AppFlow's overview names SaaS apps as sources, and the Firehose database preview ended

options.label: Events already in Kafka or Kinesis
options.why: you already have an event stream

options.label: A mix of databases and SaaS apps
options.why: you need SaaS apps too, and OLake Go moves databases, not SaaS apps

options.label: Redshift
options.why: you load Redshift, and OLake Go writes Iceberg and Parquet

options.label: Iceberg tables on S3
options.why: you want Iceberg, and these tools document a route to Iceberg tables

options.label: We write Spark or Python code
options.why: Glue needs Spark code and your team writes it

options.label: No code, the vendor runs it
options.why: you want no code and no servers

options.label: We host it ourselves
options.why: Airbyte Core is free to self-host and OLake Go is open source, and you run both yourself

options.label: An AWS service is fine
options.why: you want to stay with AWS services

questions.q: How fresh must database changes be?

options.label: Close to continuous
options.why: you want changes to land quickly, and these tools read database logs or streams, or list short sync intervals

questions.hint: Check how each tool bills before you pick.

options.label: Small and pay as I go
options.why: AppFlow bills per run and gigabyte, so a small flow costs cents

options.label: A posted monthly plan
options.why: Hevo and Airbyte Cloud post plan prices

options.label: Free software, my own servers
options.why: Airbyte Core and OLake Go are free to self-host

glue.name: AWS Glue
glue.summary: Serverless Spark jobs with the Glue Data Catalog, billed in DPU-hours.
glue.bestWhen: your team writes Spark or Python and your data already lives in AWS.
glue.watchOut: we found no native log-based CDC for self-managed databases in its docs, a job needs at least 2 DPUs, and its pricing page shows no free tier for ETL jobs.

dms.name: AWS DMS
dms.summary: A managed service that copies a database, then keeps it current from the database logs.
dms.bestWhen: you want to move or mirror a live database inside AWS.
dms.watchOut: its target list names S3, Kinesis, Kafka and others but not Iceberg, and AWS says there are no SLAs for CDC latency.

zeroetl.name: AWS Glue zero-ETL
zeroetl.summary: Managed integrations that replicate SaaS apps and DynamoDB, built to minimize pipeline code.
zeroetl.bestWhen: your sources are supported SaaS apps or DynamoDB, or a self-managed database going to Redshift.
zeroetl.watchOut: for self-managed databases the docs say you can replicate only to a Redshift data warehouse, and ingestion from applications bills $1.50 per GB (US East, Ohio).

appflow.name: Amazon AppFlow
appflow.summary: Managed SaaS-to-AWS flows, billed per flow run and per gigabyte.
appflow.bestWhen: a handful of SaaS apps need to land in S3 or Redshift.
appflow.watchOut: its overview names SaaS apps as sources, not databases, and does not mention Iceberg.

firehose.name: Amazon Data Firehose
firehose.summary: A delivery service for streaming records into S3, Redshift or Iceberg tables.
firehose.bestWhen: events already flow through Kafka or Kinesis.
firehose.watchOut: the database-as-source preview ended on 30 September 2025, and you manage compaction on self-managed Iceberg tables.

olake.name: OLake Go
olake.summary: Open-source replication with change capture for Postgres, MySQL/MariaDB, MongoDB and SQL Server (Oracle, Db2, S3 and Kafka load without it), writing Iceberg or Parquet.
olake.bestWhen: your sources are databases and you want Iceberg or Parquet on storage you run.
olake.watchOut: its output is Iceberg and Parquet, so it suits teams that want one of those on storage they run.

fivetran.name: Fivetran
fivetran.summary: A managed ELT service that says it runs the pipelines for you, with many connectors, billed on monthly active rows.
fivetran.bestWhen: you want the vendor to run everything and your row counts are predictable.
fivetran.watchOut: busy tables push the bill up, and the rates sit in a separate Service Consumption Table.

airbyte.name: Airbyte
airbyte.summary: ELT with a 700+ connector list, a self-hosted Core edition (free under the Elastic License 2.0) and a paid cloud.
airbyte.bestWhen: you want connector choice and can host it yourself, or you like a low entry price on Cloud.
airbyte.watchOut: database change capture runs as scheduled syncs, not a continuous stream, per Airbyte's docs, and Core needs servers and staff.

hevo.name: Hevo
hevo.summary: A managed ELT service with posted tiers, billed on events.
hevo.bestWhen: a small team loads Redshift and wants posted prices.
hevo.watchOut: the only Iceberg route we found in its docs is an Early Access Snowflake one, and busy tables eat event quota fast.
